Yea
yā
adv. (affirmative and intensive; rendering Hebrew 'aph, gam, and ken, Greek nai)
From Saxon gea, yes. In the Authorized Version it does two things: it affirms (Yea, yea), and far more often it intensifies, adding a second and stronger statement to one already made — not only this, but even this.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Yea is chiefly an intensive. It marks the moment a sentence goes further than it had promised to go. God tells Abraham of Sarah, “I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations” (Genesis 17:16) — the blessing said once, then said again and enlarged. Proverbs uses it to climb from strength to knowledge: “A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength” (Proverbs 24:5). Jeremiah uses it to press an indictment past what the hearer expected: prophet and priest are profane, “yea, in my house have I found their wickedness” (Jeremiah 23:11) — the corruption reaching into the temple itself. Simeon uses it to add to a mother's joy a warning she could not have wanted: “(Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,)” (Luke 2:35). As a simple affirmative the word stands in Christ's command about oaths, “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay”, where the doubling is not an oath but the plainness that makes oaths unnecessary.

Webster 1828 Definition

An affirmative particle, yes; but in Scripture chiefly an intensive, adding a second and stronger clause to the first — yea, I will bless her; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness.

expand to see more

YEA, adv. [Sax. gea.] Yes; a word expressing affirmation or assent.

2. It is used to enforce or intensify what has been said; not only so, but more; as, yea, and more also.

3. It is opposed to nay, as yes is to no.

4. YEA, n. An affirmative vote; as, the yeas and nays.

5. In Scripture, yea, I will bless her, Gen. 17; let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay, Matt. 5.

Key Scripture

Genesis 17:16 — "And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her."

Proverbs 24:5 — "A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength."

Jeremiah 23:11 — "For both prophet and priest are profane; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness, saith the LORD."

Matthew 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Modern Corruption

Christ's rule that speech be simply yea or nay is broken not only by profane swearing but by the whole apparatus of emphatic assurance — I swear, honestly, to be perfectly frank — by which a man signals that his ordinary word is worth less.

expand to see more

The Lord's point in Matthew 5:33-37 is not that oaths are always unlawful; He Himself answered under oath before the high priest, Paul calls God to record upon his soul, and God swears by Himself. The point is that a man whose plain word can be trusted has no need of an escalating scale of assurances. The scribes had built exactly such a scale, grading oaths by their object so that the weaker ones could be broken; Christ abolishes the scale and requires that the ordinary sentence carry full weight. Whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

The habit worth examining is not blasphemy but padding. Every phrase a man adds to make himself believed — I promise, trust me, I really mean it — is an admission that his unadorned speech is not sufficient security, and the more such phrases he uses the less any of them will finally be worth. The remedy is not a rule about vocabulary but a reputation: say what is so, do what was said, and let the yea stand alone. The Confession permits lawful oaths where a magistrate or a solemn occasion requires them, and warns that they are not to be used lightly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew has several intensives rendered yea — 'aph (also, indeed, yea), gam (also, moreover), and ken (so, thus) — while Greek uses nai for the plain affirmative.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'aph (H637) — also, yea, indeed; the commonest intensive, adding force to what precedes.

Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover, even; joins a further and usually stronger clause.

Hebrew ken (H3651) — so, thus, rightly; used affirmatively of what is right or true.

Greek nai (G3483) — yea, verily, truly; the plain affirmative of Matthew 5:37.

Saxon gea — yes; the Old English affirmative that gives the English word.

Usage

"Of a blessing repeated and enlarged: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations (Genesis 17:16)."

"Of an indictment pressed further than expected: yea, in my house have I found their wickedness (Jeremiah 23:11)."

"Of speech that needs no oath to support it: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Matthew 5:37)."
